summary: This experimental memo defines BinaryTime, a new ASN.1 type that represents date and time as a number. It also defines a binary-signing-time attribute for CMS as an alternative to the signing-time attribute. It was replaced by RFC 6019.

eli5.summary: Instead of writing a date in words, this writes it as a plain number that computers can compare easily. It was later replaced by RFC 6019.

subtitle: Representing dates and times as integers in ASN.1

tldr.problem: Traditional ASN.1 time formats (UTCTime and GeneralizedTime) are verbose and complex to compare, especially across time zones. Systems need a more compact and efficient way to represent signing times.
tldr.mechanism: BinaryTime represents date and time as a single integer: the number of seconds since January 1, 1970, UTC. The RFC also defines a binary-signing-time attribute for use in cryptographic message signatures.
tldr.outcome: This was an experimental proposal offering efficiency gains for systems where native integer time representation exists. RFC 6019 obsoleted it, indicating the approach did not gain wide adoption.

today: RFC 4049 is marked Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 6019. It did not achieve widespread adoption in practice.

sections.title: Introduction to BinaryTime
sections.content:
RFC 4049 introduces BinaryTime, a new ASN.1 type for representing dates and times as an integer value. Instead of using text-based formats like UTCTime or GeneralizedTime, BinaryTime lets systems represent time as a simple number.

The RFC also defines a binary-signing-time attribute for use in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), which is used to sign documents and messages. This attribute can replace the traditional signing-time attribute, taking advantage of BinaryTime's simplicity.
sections.eli5: BinaryTime is a way to write dates as numbers instead of text, making them easier for computers to work with and compare.

sections.title: The BinaryTime Format
sections.content:
A BinaryTime value is defined simply as an integer starting from zero. The integer represents the number of seconds since midnight UTC on January 1, 1970 (also called the Unix epoch), excluding leap seconds.

The encoding uses a variable-length ASN.1 integer representation. For dates up to January 19, 2038 at 03:14:07 UTC, four octets suffice (matching a 32-bit signed integer). For later dates, longer values are used—a five-octet value can represent any date for the next seventeen thousand years. The specification requires that the first octet and bit 8 of the second octet not both be all ones or all zeros, ensuring the most compact representation.
sections.eli5: A BinaryTime is just a number counting seconds from January 1, 1970. The bigger the number, the later the date. Early dates fit in 4 bytes, but later dates need 5 bytes or more.

sections.title: The Binary Signing-Time Attribute
sections.content:
CMS uses attributes to attach metadata to signed or authenticated messages. The traditional signing-time attribute records when a signature was created. The binary-signing-time attribute does the same job using a BinaryTime value instead of text.

The attribute is identified by the object identifier id-aa-binarySigningTime. It must have exactly one value—no zero values and no multiple values. In SignedData and AuthenticatedData structures, there must not be multiple instances of this attribute, and it must be a signed or authenticated attribute (not an unsigned one).
sections.eli5: When a document is signed, the signature includes a timestamp showing when it was signed. Binary-signing-time is a way to store that timestamp as a number instead of text.

sections.title: Why BinaryTime Matters
sections.content:
BinaryTime offers several advantages over traditional ASN.1 time formats. First, it is more compact: a single integer is smaller than the text representation of UTCTime or GeneralizedTime. Second, on operating systems that natively represent time as an integer, BinaryTime requires little or no conversion—the value can be used directly with simple operations like addition or division if the epoch or granularity differs. Third, comparing two BinaryTime values is straightforward: integer comparison works correctly regardless of the time zones involved, whereas comparing GeneralizedTime values across zones requires converting their text representations.

However, RFC 4049 is marked Experimental and was obsoleted by RFC 6019. This indicates the format did not achieve widespread adoption despite its theoretical advantages.
sections.eli5: A number is easier to store, faster to compare, and needs less translation than a time written in words. But this idea did not catch on as much as hoped, so a newer RFC replaced it.
